newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Ansett, Singapore Airlines seen in pact.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Ansett, Singapore Airlines seen in pact.

text.p: Australia's struggling Ansett Airlines is expected on Friday to join forces with one of the world's most profitable carriers, Singapore Airlines (SIA), in an effort to get its bottom line airborne.
After weeks of speculation that SIA will form an alliance or even buy into Ansett, the Australian airline said on Thursday it would be making a joint announcement with SIA on Friday morning.
Ansett's 50-percent shareholder, Air New Zealand, will also attend the news conference.
"There will be an alliance announcement tomorrow," the general manager of Ansett's fledgling international operations, Craig Wallace, told reporters in Melbourne.
He declined to give details, but aviation analysts said the announcement could range from a simple code-sharing and joint-marketing deal to SIA buying a one-third stake in Ansett.
The Australian Financial Review newspaper reported this week that a one-third shareholding would cost SIA A$200 million (US$150 million) to A$300 million.
If confirmed on Friday, such an equity injection into Ansett would leave SIA, Air New Zealand and Ansett's other shareholder, media group News Corp each with equal stakes.

News currently own 50 percent of Ansett Holdings Ltd, which in turn owns 100 percent of Ansett's domestic Australian operations and 49 percent of Ansett International. The rest of Ansett International is owned by Australian institutions.
Ansett is heavily geared and has been trading in the red in recent years.
It is expected to report a break-even profit result for the year ending June 30, but analysts said earnings were unlikely to take off until they team up with another airline like SIA.
"They (Ansett) have to do it," a Sydney-based analyst told Reuters.
"The balance sheet of Ansett is an absolute debacle. Their debt is so high they need someone else to find to repair it," said another analyst who declined to be identified.
An alliance would also benefit SIA, through better and more efficient coverage in Australia and reinforcing Singapore as a hub for airline travel between Australia and Europe, the analysts said.

If its takes an equity stake, SIA also stands to benefit if Ansett executive chairman Rod Eddington achieves his goal of turning Ansett around in three years and getting it in shape for an eventual listing on the Australian share market, they said.

Air New Zealand also stands to gain capacity through Asia to Europe, one analyst said. "Air New Zealand fly to London the other way -- they go through the United States -- so this does give them a new product offering," one analyst said.

Under code-sharing deals, airlines use each other's seats and can boost their capacity cheaply. Under Ansett's existing alliance with Air New Zealand, the two airlines also plan to share maintenance and other costs.
Ansett's arch rival, Qantas Airways Ltd, which is 25 percent owned by British Airways, has threatened to respond aggressively to an alliance between SIA, Ansett and Air New Zealand.
"I can't predict our attitude towards it, other than it will be aggressive," Qantas chief executive James Strong told reporters on Thursday.
